cards.front: About 99 percent of the calcium in an adult human body is in {{c1::bone}}.
cards.back: The parathyroid glands read only a sliver of the remaining 1 percent: the free calcium ions in plasma.
cards.quote: About 99 percent of the calcium in an adult human body is in bone, yet the parathyroid glands read only a sliver

cards.front: In adult human calcium control, what is the regulated variable, and how is PTH set from it?
cards.back: Plasma ionized calcium. The parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor reads it and sets PTH by negative feedback: less calcium, more PTH.
cards.quote: The parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor reads it and sets PTH by negative feedback: less calcium, more PTH.

cards.front: Name the three doors through which PTH raises plasma calcium, with the clock each runs on.
cards.back: Kidney reabsorption (minutes); bone resorption (hours for the first release, days for new osteoclasts); gut absorption via calcitriol that PTH has the kidney make (a day or more).
cards.quote: PTH opens three doors that raise plasma calcium, each on its own clock: kidney reabsorption (minutes)

cards.front: In round numbers, about 14 L of extracellular fluid holds filterable calcium at 60 mg per L, and the kidneys filter about 10,800 mg of calcium a day. Roughly how often does the whole filterable stock pass the glomerular filter?
cards.back: Stock = 14 L x 60 mg per L = 840 mg. 840 / 10,800 per day = 0.078 day, about 1.9 hours: roughly once every two hours, so almost all of it must be reabsorbed.
cards.quote: the whole stock passes the filter roughly once every two hours, and almost all of it has to come back

cards.front: Plasma calcium in an adult human sits in three pockets. Give each with its approximate share of the total.
cards.back: Free ionized, roughly half; protein-bound, mostly albumin, about 40 percent; complexed with citrate, phosphate and bicarbonate, about 10 percent.
cards.why: Only the ionized fraction acts on cells and is sensed and regulated.
cards.quote: Roughly half of the total is free ionized calcium, about 40 percent is bound to protein, mostly albumin, and about 10 percent is complexed with citrate, phosphate and bicarbonate.
cards.section: What is regulated: ionized calcium

cards.front: A lab reports ionized calcium of 1.1 mmol/L. Taking calcium's molar mass as about 40 g, what is this in mg/dL?
cards.back: 1 mmol/L is about 4 mg/dL, so 1.1 mmol/L x 4 = about 4.4 mg/dL.
cards.quote: Calcium's molar mass is about 40 g, so 1 mmol/L is about 4 mg/dL
cards.section: What is regulated: ionized calcium

cards.front: A person hyperventilates into respiratory alkalosis. Predict total and ionized plasma calcium, and the likely symptom.
cards.back: Total calcium stays the same; ionized calcium falls. Fewer hydrogen ions compete for albumin, so albumin binds more calcium. Nerves and muscles become overexcitable, felt as tingling in the fingers.
cards.why: Calcium only moves from the free pocket to the albumin pocket, so a normal total can hide a drop in the regulated variable.
cards.quote: Total calcium stays the same and ionized calcium falls: calcium has only moved from the free pocket to the albumin pocket
cards.section: What is regulated: ionized calcium

cards.front: A patient develops acidosis with a normal albumin. Using the rule that hydrogen ions compete with calcium for albumin's binding sites, predict total and ionized plasma calcium.
cards.back: Total calcium unchanged; ionized calcium rises. More hydrogen ions compete for albumin, so albumin binds less calcium and some moves into the free pocket.
cards.why: This reverses the alkalosis case: only the distribution among pockets changes, not the total.
cards.quote: In alkalosis, fewer hydrogen ions compete for albumin's binding sites, so albumin binds more calcium.
cards.section: What is regulated: ionized calcium

cards.front: Parathyroid chief cells carry the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), a {{c1::G protein-coupled receptor}} that binds ionized calcium outside the cell.
cards.back: High calcium keeps the receptor active and PTH secretion down.
cards.quote: Their chief cells carry the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), a G protein-coupled receptor (G proteins) that binds ionized calcium outside the cell.
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: Why does the steepness of the parathyroid CaSR response to calcium matter for plasma calcium?
cards.back: A small change in ionized calcium moves PTH a long way, which keeps plasma calcium in a narrow range.
cards.quote: The response is steep, so a small change in calcium moves PTH a long way, which keeps the range narrow.
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: What kind of hormone is PTH, and what second messenger does its receptor raise?
cards.back: A peptide. It acts through a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP.
cards.quote: It acts through a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP (cAMP and PKA).
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: PTH raises bone resorption, yet its receptors are not mainly on osteoclasts. How does it reach them?
cards.back: PTH receptors sit on osteoblast-lineage cells, including osteocytes. These raise RANKL relative to its decoy OPG, so more osteoclasts form.
cards.quote: PTH's receptors sit on osteoblast-lineage cells, including osteocytes, so PTH reaches osteoclasts mainly through them
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: Why is the gut door of PTH's calcium response the slowest, at a day or more?
cards.back: PTH acts through calcitriol, which works via the vitamin D receptor, a transcription factor. Its effect waits on new proteins being made.
cards.quote: Calcitriol acts through the vitamin D receptor, a transcription factor (nuclear receptors), so its effect waits on new proteins.
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: PTH dissolves bone mineral, which is calcium phosphate. When PTH rises in an adult with working kidneys, which way does plasma phosphate go, and why?
cards.back: Down. At the proximal tubule PTH pulls the cotransporter NaPi-IIa out of the brush border, so less filtered phosphate is reabsorbed and more is lost in urine.
cards.why: The kidney's extra excretion outweighs the phosphate released from bone.
cards.quote: It pulls the sodium-phosphate cotransporter NaPi-IIa out of the proximal tubule's brush border, so less filtered phosphate is reabsorbed and more is lost in urine.
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: Illustrative adult: GFR 180 L per day, plasma phosphate 33 mg per L, 90 percent filterable. PTH raises fractional excretion of phosphate from 15 to 20 percent, while extra bone resorption adds about 90 mg of phosphate a day. Compare the two.
cards.back: Filtered phosphate = 180 x 33 x 0.9 = 5,346 mg per day. Extra excreted = 0.05 x 5,346 = about 270 mg per day, versus about 90 mg added from bone. The kidney wins: phosphate falls.
cards.quote: The kidneys filter about 5,300 mg of phosphate a day (180 L × 33 mg per L × 90 percent filterable)
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: Give the three organs, in order, that make calcitriol from vitamin D.
cards.back: Skin makes vitamin D, the liver 25-hydroxylates it, and the kidney 1-hydroxylates it, giving calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D).
cards.quote: 25-hydroxylated in the liver (absorption and the liver) and 1-hydroxylated in the kidney, giving calcitriol, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: What are calcitriol's two jobs in the calcium loop?
cards.back: It is PTH's slow arm, raising gut absorption of calcium and phosphate. It also suppresses PTH gene transcription, so a hormone PTH makes turns PTH down.
cards.quote: Second, it suppresses PTH gene transcription, so a hormone PTH makes turns PTH down.
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: Where is calcitonin made, what does it do to isolated osteoclasts, and how important is it in normal adult humans?
cards.back: Thyroid parafollicular C cells. It stops the crawling of isolated osteoclasts within minutes, yet its role in normal adult human calcium control appears modest.
cards.quote: yet its role in normal adult human calcium control appears modest
cards.section: One sensor, one hormone, three doors

cards.front: Which fractions of plasma calcium are filtered at the glomerulus, and roughly what share of the total is that?
cards.back: The ionized and complexed fractions, roughly 55 to 60 percent of total. Protein-bound calcium is not filtered.
cards.quote: Protein-bound calcium is not filtered; the ionized and complexed fractions, roughly 55 to 60 percent of total, are.
cards.section: The kidney door, in numbers

cards.front: Along the nephron, where is filtered calcium reabsorbed, and at which step does PTH do most of its fine-tuning?
cards.back: Proximal tubule 60 to 70 percent; thick ascending limb 20 to 25 percent, largely between cells; distal convoluted and connecting tubules 5 to 10 percent through cells. PTH fine-tunes the distal step.
cards.quote: The distal convoluted and connecting tubules take back roughly 5 to 10 percent through cells, the step where PTH does most of its fine-tuning.
cards.section: The kidney door, in numbers

cards.front: The distal nephron reabsorbs 5 to 10 percent of a filtered calcium load of about 10,800 mg a day. Compare that with a daily urinary calcium of about 200 mg.
cards.back: 0.05 to 0.10 x 10,800 = 540 to 1,080 mg a day, about 2.7 to 5.4 times urinary calcium. The regulated step is small next to what is filtered and large next to what is lost.
cards.quote: But 5 to 10 percent of about 10,800 mg a day is 540 to 1,080 mg
cards.section: The kidney door, in numbers

cards.front: Made-up adult at steady state: GFR 120 mL per min, total plasma calcium 9 mg per dL, 60 percent filterable, urinary calcium 250 mg per day. Find the filtered load and the fraction reabsorbed.
cards.back: GFR = 0.12 L per min x 1,440 = 172.8 L per day. Filterable calcium = 90 x 0.6 = 54 mg per L. Filtered load = 9,331 mg per day. FE = 250 / 9,331 = 2.7 percent, so about 97.3 percent is reabsorbed.
cards.quote: Filtered load = 180 x 60 = 10,800 mg per day.
cards.section: Worked problem: calcium and phosphate in a day

cards.front: Made-up adult at steady state with bone formation equal to resorption and no sweat losses: calcium intake 1,200 mg per day, urinary calcium 180 mg per day. What is fecal calcium?
cards.back: With bone in balance, net intestinal absorption equals urinary excretion, 180 mg per day. Fecal calcium = 1,200 - 180 = 1,020 mg per day.
cards.quote: With bone in balance, net intestinal absorption equals urinary excretion, 200 mg per day.
cards.section: Worked problem: calcium and phosphate in a day

cards.front: Filtered calcium load 10,800 mg per day, urinary calcium 200 mg per day. As a what-if, fractional reabsorption falls from 98.15 to 97.5 percent with the filtered load held fixed. New urinary calcium?
cards.back: Excretion = 10,800 x 0.025 = 270 mg per day, 1.35 times the original: a fall of 0.65 percentage points in reabsorption raises excretion by 35 percent.
cards.why: The small regulated step acts on a huge flow.
cards.quote: a fall of about 1.15 percentage points in reabsorption moves excretion by 62 percent, because the small regulated step acts on a huge flow
cards.section: Worked problem: calcium and phosphate in a day

cards.front: In life, PTH usually falls because plasma calcium rose. Name three effects of that calcium rise that each raise urinary calcium.
cards.back: It raises the filtered load, switches off PTH (less distal reabsorption), and acts on CaSR in the thick ascending limb to lower reabsorption there.
cards.quote: In life PTH usually falls because calcium rose, and a rise in calcium raises the filtered load, switches off PTH and acts on CaSR in the thick ascending limb.
cards.section: Worked problem: calcium and phosphate in a day

cards.front: Fractional excretion of phosphate: FE(P) = phosphate clearance / {{c1::creatinine clearance}}.
cards.back: Creatinine clearance is taken as an estimate of GFR.
cards.quote: Step 3, FE(P) = phosphate clearance / creatinine clearance
cards.section: Worked problem: calcium and phosphate in a day

cards.front: Made-up values from a blood sample and spot urine taken together: plasma phosphate 2.0 mg per dL, urine phosphate 10 mg per dL, plasma creatinine 1.0 mg per dL, urine creatinine 100 mg per dL. Find FE(P). Is the kidney conserving phosphate, against a reference of about 15 percent?
cards.back: FE(P) = (10 x 1.0) / (2.0 x 100) = 10 / 200 = 5 percent. Below 15 percent, so this kidney is holding on to phosphate.
cards.quote: This lesson's reference adult, with normal phosphate, excretes about 15 percent of filtered phosphate, and a kidney conserving phosphate should excrete less than that.
cards.section: Worked problem: calcium and phosphate in a day

cards.front: Why can FE(P) be calculated from a spot urine without knowing urine flow, and what does the method assume?
cards.back: Urine flow V appears in both phosphate and creatinine clearance and cancels. It assumes creatinine clearance approximates GFR, phosphate is freely filtered, and both samples are taken together.
cards.quote: V is on top and bottom and cancels, which is why a spot urine works.
cards.section: Worked problem: calcium and phosphate in a day

cards.front: An adult with low plasma phosphate has an FE(P) of 20 percent. The calculation shows renal phosphate wasting but cannot say whether PTH or FGF23 drives it. Which plasma measurement would best separate the two, and how?
cards.back: Calcitriol is one clue: PTH tends to raise it and FGF23 to lower it, so low calcitriol leans toward FGF23 and high toward PTH; stage, treatment and other disease can change this.
cards.why: Rests on the hormone table: both lower phosphate, but they act in opposite directions on calcitriol.
cards.quote: A fifth is no small fraction, so this kidney is not holding on: that points to renal phosphate wasting, for example from PTH or FGF23.
cards.section: Worked problem: calcium and phosphate in a day

cards.front: Name the three bone cells and what each does.
cards.back: Osteoblasts lay down matrix; osteoclasts resorb it; osteocytes are former osteoblasts walled into the matrix, linked to one another by fine processes.
cards.quote: Osteoblasts lay down matrix, osteoclasts resorb it, and osteocytes, former osteoblasts walled into the matrix, stay linked to one another by fine processes.
cards.section: The bone door: RANKL and OPG

cards.front: How do RANKL, RANK and osteoprotegerin (OPG) together set osteoclast number?
cards.back: RANKL on osteoblast-lineage cells and osteocytes engages RANK on osteoclast precursors, driving their formation and activation. OPG is a soluble decoy that binds RANKL and keeps it off RANK. RANKL relative to OPG is a main control.
cards.why: A key, a lock, and a dummy lock that swallows keys.
cards.quote: Osteoprotegerin (OPG) is a soluble decoy: it binds RANKL and keeps it off RANK.
cards.section: The bone door: RANKL and OPG

cards.front: Transgenic mice expressing osteoprotegerin (OPG) from the liver developed profound but nonlethal osteopetrosis. What does the result show?
cards.back: Excess decoy swallowed the RANKL keys, so too little bone was resorbed. RANKL engaging RANK is needed for normal resorption.
cards.quote: they developed profound but nonlethal osteopetrosis, an excess of dense bone, because with the keys swallowed too little bone was resorbed
cards.section: The bone door: RANKL and OPG

cards.front: RANKL is deleted specifically in mouse osteocytes. Predict bone mass and osteoclast number, and state the conclusion and its limit.
cards.back: Severe osteopetrosis with fewer osteoclasts, as two studies found. Osteocytes are a major source of the RANKL remodeling needs in mice; necessary in that setting, not the only source at every age, site or in humans.
cards.quote: So in mice osteocytes are a major source of the RANKL that remodeling needs
cards.section: The bone door: RANKL and OPG

cards.front: What does continuous PTH excess do to bone, and why should intermittent exposure not be lumped with it?
cards.back: Continuous excess causes net bone loss even though formation also rises. Intermittent exposure behaves differently from continuous excess, so the continuous-excess result should not be applied to it.
cards.quote: Continuous PTH excess causes net bone loss even though formation also rises; intermittent exposure behaves differently and should not be lumped with it.
cards.section: The bone door: RANKL and OPG

cards.front: Which cells make FGF23, and through what receptor complex does it act on the kidney?
cards.back: Osteocytes and osteoblasts. It acts through an FGF receptor paired with the co-receptor Klotho.
cards.quote: Osteocytes and osteoblasts make FGF23, which acts on the kidney through an FGF receptor paired with the co-receptor Klotho.
cards.section: Phosphate's own brake: FGF23

cards.front: FGF23 and PTH both lower proximal phosphate reabsorption. How do they differ at the kidney, and why does FGF23's difference suit a phosphate hormone?
cards.back: FGF23 lowers calcitriol; PTH raises it. Calcitriol raises gut phosphate absorption, so lowering it cuts phosphate intake at the source.
cards.quote: It does two things there: it lowers phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, as PTH does; it lowers calcitriol, the opposite of PTH.
cards.section: Phosphate's own brake: FGF23

cards.front: What mainly controls FGF23 secretion, and why is it called a phosphate hormone rather than an arm of the calcium response?
cards.back: Mainly phosphate and calcitriol, not the calcium-sensing receptor. Calcitriol raises FGF23, and FGF23 lowers calcitriol: a second, smaller loop running on phosphate.
cards.quote: FGF23 answers mainly to phosphate and calcitriol, not to the calcium-sensing receptor
cards.section: Phosphate's own brake: FGF23

cards.front: Mice with Fgf23 deleted are compared with littermates. What were serum phosphate, renal phosphate reabsorption and calcitriol, and what does the result show?
cards.back: Phosphate high, renal phosphate reabsorption increased, calcitriol elevated, with abnormal bone mineralization. Endogenous FGF23 is necessary for normal phosphate and vitamin D handling in the mouse.
cards.why: A lifelong whole-body deletion cannot separate direct renal effects from those of high calcitriol or development.
cards.quote: Compared with littermates, the null mice had high serum phosphate, increased renal phosphate reabsorption and elevated calcitriol, with abnormal bone mineralization.
cards.section: The modern experiment: mice without FGF23

cards.front: Recombinant FGF23 is injected into parathyroidectomized rats and serum phosphate falls. What does using parathyroidectomized animals establish?
cards.back: FGF23's phosphate-lowering effect does not need PTH.
cards.quote: recombinant FGF23 lowered serum phosphate even in parathyroidectomized rats, so that effect did not need PTH
cards.section: The modern experiment: mice without FGF23

cards.front: A tumor secretes large amounts of FGF23 in an adult with working kidneys. Predict plasma phosphate, FE(P) and calcitriol.
cards.back: FE(P) high (renal phosphate wasting), plasma phosphate low, calcitriol low or inappropriately low.
cards.why: FGF23 lowers proximal phosphate reabsorption and lowers calcitriol, which also cuts gut phosphate absorption.
cards.quote: FGF23 was first tied to rare disorders in which too much FGF23 activity makes the kidney lose phosphate.
cards.section: The modern experiment: mice without FGF23

cards.front: In untreated primary hyperparathyroidism, PTH raises distal calcium reabsorption. Why can urinary calcium still be raised?
cards.back: Plasma calcium rises, so the filtered calcium load rises, and more calcium reaches the urine despite the extra distal reabsorption.
cards.quote: Urinary calcium can still be raised, because plasma calcium and so the filtered load rise.
cards.section: Predicting the disorders from the loop

cards.front: After neck surgery, an adult's parathyroid glands no longer secrete PTH. Predict plasma calcium, phosphate, PTH and calcitriol, and explain the phosphate.
cards.back: Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH low or inappropriately low, calcitriol low or low-normal. Without PTH phosphaturia the kidney keeps phosphate it would have thrown out.
cards.quote: Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH low or inappropriately low, calcitriol low or low-normal.
cards.section: Predicting the disorders from the loop

cards.front: In early vitamin D deficiency, vitamin D stores are low. Why can calcitriol be normal or even high, and what happens to phosphate?
cards.back: PTH rises, and high PTH stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylation, so calcitriol can be normal or high. The same PTH throws out phosphate, so phosphate is often normal and can be low.
cards.quote: The loop compensates: PTH rises, and high PTH stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylation, so calcitriol can be normal or even high.
cards.section: Predicting the disorders from the loop

cards.front: Illustrative adult with CKD: GFR 90 L per day, 800 mg a day of phosphate absorbed, 90 percent of plasma phosphate filterable. What FE(P) keeps plasma phosphate at 3.3 mg/dL (33 mg per L)?
cards.back: At steady state, intake = GFR x 0.9 x plasma phosphate x FE(P). FE(P) = 800 / (90 x 0.9 x 33) = 800 / 2,673 = about 0.30, or 30 percent.
cards.quote: Turned around, plasma phosphate = intake ÷ (GFR × 0.9 × FE(P))
cards.section: Predicting the disorders from the loop

cards.front: In advanced CKD (GFR 15 L per day, 800 mg a day of phosphate absorbed), why does plasma phosphate stay high despite high PTH?
cards.back: FE(P) cannot exceed 100 percent. Even excreting every filtered milligram, plasma phosphate = 800 / (15 x 0.9 x 1.0) = about 59 mg per L, near 5.9 mg/dL. PTH's phosphate-lowering signature fails when the kidney cannot excrete.
cards.quote: FE(P) stops at 100 percent, and at a GFR of 15 L per day excreting every filtered milligram still leaves plasma phosphate near 5.9 mg/dL.
cards.section: Predicting the disorders from the loop

cards.front: A large cross-sectional cohort of adults with CKD finds FGF23 elevated while phosphate and PTH are still normal. What does this support, and what can it not prove?
cards.back: It fits FGF23 rising first, raising FE(P) to keep phosphate normal. Being cross-sectional, it cannot prove the order of the changes. Here still normal means mean phosphate and median PTH; the cohort was nearly all CKD stages 2 to 4.
cards.quote: which fits FGF23 rising first without proving the order
cards.section: Predicting the disorders from the loop

cards.front: Adult mice with inducible osteocyte RANKL deletion and controls all receive continuous PTH. Calcium rises in the first hours in both groups, but deleted mice add no osteoclasts and fall behind over days. Interpret.
cards.back: The slow part of the bone door, new osteoclast formation, needs osteocyte RANKL; the early release from bone surfaces does not. The result applies to mice in this setting.
cards.quote: If calcium rises in the first hours in both groups but the deleted mice add no osteoclasts and fall behind over days
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Illustrative adult: GFR 180 L per day, 90 percent filterable, phosphate input 800 mg a day at FE(P) 15 percent. PTH adds 200 mg a day of input (bone plus gut). What FE(P) must PTH reach just to keep plasma phosphate from rising?
cards.back: Baseline phosphate = 800 / (180 x 0.9 x 0.15) = about 32.9 mg per L. Break-even FE(P) = 1,000 / (180 x 0.9 x 32.9) = about 0.19, or 19 percent.
cards.why: PTH lowers phosphate only because its effect on excretion is large.
cards.quote: PTH lowers phosphate because its effect on excretion is large, not automatically.
cards.section: How large PTH's phosphate effect must be

cards.front: Mice lacking the vitamin D receptor get rickets and high PTH. A high-calcium, high-phosphate diet with lactose restores ionized calcium and prevents both. What does this point to?
cards.back: Impaired intestinal calcium absorption as the cause of the rickets and the PTH rise.
cards.quote: That points to impaired intestinal calcium absorption as the cause (Li and colleagues, 1998).
cards.section: The experiments behind the kidney and gut steps

cards.front: Ligaments join bone to bone and {{c1::tendons}} join muscle to bone.
cards.quote: Ligaments join bone to bone and tendons join muscle to bone.
cards.section: Bone as a tissue, and the joints
